1. Introduction

Scientific publishing is the backbone of evidence-based medicine, public policy, and technological progress. However, the system is under severe stress: over 10,000 peer-reviewed papers were retracted in 2023 alone, a fourfold increase from a decade earlier. Commercial “paper mills” now industrially generate fraudulent manuscripts, manipulate peer review through compromised reviewer accounts, and fabricate data at scale. The consequences are real—retracted papers on drug efficacy have entered clinical guidelines, retracted engineering studies have informed infrastructure design, and over 95% of citations to retracted papers occur after the retraction notice is published.

The traditional peer-review system, relying on volunteer referees who invest fewer than five hours per manuscript on average, is inadequate against organized fraud syndicates. The median time from publication to official retraction is 2.8 to 4.1 years, during which the flawed findings propagate through downstream citations and meta-analyses.

RetractGuard is our response to this challenge. It is an end-to-end machine learning system that evaluates publication metadata, author behavioural histories, and citation network topology to output calibrated retraction risk scores—without requiring full manuscript textual inspection. By triangulating data from three authoritative bibliometric sources (Retraction Watch, OpenAlex, and Crossref), we engineer 12 domain-specific features and train, regularize, tune, and ensemble multiple classifiers, evaluating them under realistic class imbalance using Precision-Recall AUC as the primary metric.

2. Problem Statement

To build a classification model that identifies scholarly papers at elevated risk of future retraction based on authorship patterns, citation behaviour, and journal-level metadata; to engineer meaningful features from raw bibliometric and network data; and to compare multiple classification and ensemble approaches under class imbalance, using appropriate metrics to evaluate real-world applicability for research-integrity screening.

2.1 Specific Objectives

  1. Integrate three heterogeneous bibliometric data sources—Retraction Watch (Kaggle, 52,982 retracted records), OpenAlex REST API (250M+ scholarly works), and Crossref REST API (editorial timestamps)—into a unified, leakage-free analytical corpus.
  2. Derive 12 domain-grounded features spanning author history, citation dynamics, co-authorship graph topology, and editorial process characteristics, with mathematical justification for each.
  3. Implement and compare baseline classifiers (Logistic Regression, Decision Trees), regularized variants (L1 Lasso, L2 Ridge, Cost-Complexity Pruning), and ensemble methods (Random Forest Bagging, XGBoost Boosting, Soft Stacking) under SMOTE-balanced, stratified cross-validation pipelines.
  4. Conduct systematic hyperparameter optimization using 5-fold Stratified RandomizedSearchCV, optimizing Precision-Recall AUC to avoid the accuracy paradox under severe class imbalance.
  5. Deploy the best-performing model (Tuned XGBoost, PR-AUC = 0.836) as a Flask REST API with a React + Tailwind CSS dark-mode frontend for interactive demonstration on curated Retraction Watch preset papers.

2.2 Scope and Constraints

  • The system operates on metadata only—no full-text, image, or supplementary material analysis is performed. This is both a design choice (metadata is openly available) and a limitation (image duplication and text plagiarism are not detected).
  • Temporal data leakage is strictly prevented: author retraction histories are computed only from events prior to each paper’s publication date, and journal retraction rates are computed strictly within cross-validation training folds.
  • The final model is calibrated for a screening (triage) workflow, not for definitive retraction adjudication. False positives are routed to human reviewers for further investigation.

The following table summarizes earlier work on retraction prediction and the Retraction Watch dataset, situating our contributions within the existing literature:

Study / System Year Dataset Used Methodology Key Results Limitation Addressed by Our Work
Grieneisen & Zhang, “A Comprehensive Survey of Retracted Articles from the Scholarly Literature” 2012 PubMed + manual curation Descriptive statistics; temporal trend analysis Identified exponential growth in retractions; dominant misconduct categories No predictive model; purely observational. We build a classification pipeline.
Fang, Steen & Casadevall, “Misconduct accounts for the majority of retracted scientific publications” 2012 PubMed (2,047 retracted articles) Manual re-examination of retraction notices 67.4% of retractions due to misconduct (not error); strong journal-tier pattern Manual coding is non-scalable. Our system automates feature extraction via APIs.
Bhatt (Kaggle), “Retraction Watch EDA” 2021 Retraction Watch (Kaggle) Exploratory Data Analysis; visualizations of reasons, countries, publishers Top retraction reasons: fabrication, plagiarism, duplication; publisher concentration EDA only, no ML classification. We extend to full predictive modeling.
Cokol et al., “Retraction rates are on the rise” 2008 PubMed retraction notices Statistical analysis of retraction rates over time Retraction rate growing faster than publication rate; field-dependent patterns No feature engineering from citation networks. We add graph topology features.
Didegah & Gazni, “Predicting article citations using metadata” 2023 OpenAlex / Scopus metadata Random Forest, Gradient Boosting on bibliometric features Author history and journal prestige are strong citation predictors Predicts citations, not retractions. We repurpose similar features for integrity screening.
Priem et al., “OpenAlex: A fully-open index of scholarly works” 2022 OpenAlex database documentation System paper describing API design and coverage 250M+ works, fully open, superior DOI coverage vs. MAG Infrastructure paper. We operationalize OpenAlex as a live feature-extraction API.
Retraction Watch Foundation 2018–present Retraction Watch Database Manual curation, journalist investigation Maintained the largest curated retraction database (52k+ events) Human-curated registry. We use it as ground-truth labels for ML classification.

Our contribution relative to prior work: We are the first to combine the Retraction Watch ground-truth labels with live OpenAlex citation-graph features and Crossref editorial timestamps in a single leakage-free machine learning pipeline that evaluates nine model configurations (including three ensemble approaches) under class imbalance using PR-AUC as the primary metric, and deploys the winning model as a web application with preset demonstration papers.

5. Methodology

5.1 Data Preprocessing & EDA

The raw Retraction Watch CSV (52,982 rows, 20 columns, latin-1 encoding) was cleaned: invalid/missing DOIs were dropped, duplicate retraction records were deduplicated, and retraction reasons were parsed from semicolon-delimited strings. A balanced cohort of 3,750 papers (750 retracted + 3,000 year-matched clean controls sourced via OpenAlex) was constructed.

EDA Step Technique Key Finding
Class Distribution Bar chart + imbalance ratio 1:4 retracted-to-clean ratio; accuracy paradox demonstrated (trivial baseline = 80% accuracy, 0% recall)

Temporal Trends Time-series line plot by year Exponential surge post-2018 due to publisher-wide paper mill purges

5.2 Feature Engineering

12 features were derived from three API sources, with mathematical justifications documented in Notebook 01. Key formulas:

citation_velocity = cited_by_count / max(1, years_since_publication)
self_citation_ratio = |refs sharing co-author| / |total refs|
coauthor_clustering_coeff = 2 * E_i / (k_i * (k_i - 1))
coauthor_degree_centrality = deg(v) / (N - 1)

All features were engineered to be strictly leakage-free: prior_author_retractions counts only events before the target paper’s publication date, and journal_retraction_rate is computed within cross-validation training folds only.

5.3 Baseline Model Selection

Logistic Regression (Unregularized, C = 105) was selected as the baseline for two reasons: (1) it provides a linear log-odds decision boundary serving as the simplest possible parametric baseline, and (2) its coefficients are directly interpretable, enabling domain-expert validation of learned feature weights. Under SMOTE-balanced 5-fold cross-validation, it achieved PR-AUC = 0.755 and ROC-AUC = 0.907.

5.4 Models Compared

Model Category Rationale for Inclusion
Logistic Regression (Unreg.)Linear BaselineInterpretable linear log-odds boundary; establishes performance floor
Logistic Regression (L2 Ridge)Regularized LinearTests whether weight dampening improves generalization on collinear features
Logistic Regression (L1 Lasso)Regularized LinearTests automatic feature selection via sparsity induction
Decision Tree (Unpruned)Non-linear BaselineCaptures feature interactions but prone to memorization
Decision Tree (Pruned)Regularized Non-linearCost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha = 0.012) controls overfitting
Random Forest (200 trees)Bagging EnsembleReduces variance via bootstrap aggregation on noisy citation features
XGBoost (Default)Boosting EnsembleReduces bias via sequential gradient correction
XGBoost (Tuned & Regularized)Boosting + TuningFull hyperparameter optimization with L1/L2 tree regularization
Soft Stacking EnsembleMeta-EnsembleCombines linear + bagged + boosted decisions via LR meta-learner

5.5 Ensemble Methods

  • Bagging (Random Forest): 200 independent deep decision trees via bootstrap aggregation with random feature subspace sampling. Reduces variance on noisy co-authorship graph features.
  • Boosting (XGBoost): Sequential gradient boosting on pseudo-residuals with second-order Taylor expansion loss. Reduces bias on complex non-linear fraud interaction patterns.
  • Soft Stacking: Level-0 models (Logistic Regression + Random Forest + XGBoost) feed predicted probabilities into a Level-1 Logistic Regression meta-learner, blending linear and non-linear decision surfaces.

7.2 Regularization Effects

L1/L2 Regularization (Logistic Regression): L1 Lasso induced sparsity, zeroing out noisy network metrics; L2 Ridge dampened collinear author velocity coefficients. Coefficient shrinkage paths were plotted across C values from 10-4 to 103.

Cost-Complexity Pruning (Decision Trees): The unpruned tree severely overfitted (Train PR-AUC = 1.000 vs. Test PR-AUC = 0.368). Pruning with ccp_alpha = 0.012 improved test PR-AUC to 0.437 (+18.7% relative gain).

Figure 7: L1 Lasso vs. L2 Ridge coefficient shrinkage paths across regularization strength.

7.3 Cross-Validated Hyperparameter Tuning

50 iterations of RandomizedSearchCV with 5-fold Stratified CV optimizing average_precision (PR-AUC) on XGBoost:

HyperparameterDefaultTuned OptimalImpact
n_estimators100180Expanded ensemble capacity
learning_rate0.300.05Prevented aggressive updates on noise
max_depth64Constrained interaction order
subsample1.00.80Bagging-style variance reduction per tree
colsample_bytree1.00.80Decorrelated trees across feature groups
reg_alpha (L1)0.00.15Sparsity on extraneous bibliometrics
reg_lambda (L2)1.02.50Stabilized leaf weights against outliers

Tuning impact: Test PR-AUC increased from 0.813 to 0.836 (+2.3% absolute); F1 lifted from 0.672 to 0.713 (+6.1%).

9. Conclusions

  1. Effective Multi-Source Feature Engineering: By triangulating Retraction Watch ground-truth labels, OpenAlex citation-graph features, and Crossref editorial timestamps, we engineered 12 domain-grounded features that capture authorship anomalies, citation cartel dynamics, and editorial process irregularities.
  2. Class Imbalance Addressed Rigorously: The accuracy paradox was identified early, and all evaluation was anchored on PR-AUC and F1-Score. SMOTE was applied strictly within cross-validation training folds to prevent data leakage.
  3. Regularization Demonstrably Beneficial: L1/L2 coefficient shrinkage paths and cost-complexity tree pruning measurably reduced overfitting. The unpruned Decision Tree’s PR-AUC improved by 18.7% after pruning.
  4. Tuned XGBoost is the Clear Champion: After 5-fold stratified hyperparameter tuning, the regularized XGBoost achieved PR-AUC = 0.836, ROC-AUC = 0.938, and F1 = 0.713, outperforming all nine candidate configurations.
  5. Interpretable Risk Drivers: Feature importance analysis revealed that prior_author_retractions (31.4%), review_turnaround_days (22.8%), and journal_retraction_rate (14.2%) are the top three risk drivers, all of which are actionable for editorial screening.
  6. End-to-End Deployment: The winning model was serialized and deployed as a Flask REST API with a React dark-mode frontend, enabling interactive demonstration on curated Retraction Watch preset papers.

Limitations: The system relies solely on metadata and cannot detect image manipulation, text plagiarism, or data fabrication within the manuscript body. Crossref timestamp coverage is incomplete for some older papers. The model is designed for screening/triage, not for definitive retraction adjudication.

Future Work: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) over heterogeneous author-paper-venue graphs; multimodal extensions using SciBERT abstract embeddings and computer-vision-based image duplication detection; deployment as an automated pre-publication screening plugin for journal editorial management systems.
